ai.title: Disruptive Behaviour Disorders
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Disruptive behaviour disorders are persistent patterns of defiant, hostile or aggressive conduct that impair social, academic or occupational functioning. They are diagnosed by DSM‑5 criteria and managed with behavioural strategies, psychoeducation and, when needed, pharmacotherapy.

b: Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD): irritability, defiance, vindictiveness Conduct Disorder (CD): aggression, rule‑breaking, deceit ADHD + ODD: hyperactivity, inattention plus defiant behaviour
sections.p: DSM‑5 defines disruptive behaviour disorders as a persistent pattern of defiant, hostile or aggressive behaviour that violates the rights of others or major rules. Diagnosis requires at least three symptoms for 12 months, with onset before 18 years, and evidence of impairment in at least two settings.

Severity is graded by the number of symptoms, the range of settings affected and the level of functional impairment. The DSM‑5 does not provide a formal staging system, but clinicians use the following pragmatic scale: mild (few symptoms, limited impairment), moderate (multiple symptoms, moderate impairment), severe (many symptoms, significant impairment).

b: Early childhood adversity (abuse, neglect) Family conflict or parental mental illness Socio‑economic deprivation Exposure to violence or community conflict Neurodevelopmental disorders (ADHD, learning difficulties)
sections.p: Disruptive behaviour has multifactorial origins. In low‑resource settings, key contributors include:

b: Physical injury to self or others Sexual aggression Suicidal ideation Rapid escalation of conduct

Investigations aim to rule out medical or psychiatric comorbidities and to guide treatment. In low‑resource hospitals, prioritize affordable tests.

sections.p: Red flags indicating urgent care include self‑harm, severe aggression, or evidence of abuse. Complications may involve academic failure, social isolation, substance misuse, or progression to antisocial personality disorder.

b: Behavioural interventions – parent training, school support, social skills training Pharmacotherapy – when behavioural strategies fail or symptoms are severe. Preferred agents: methylphenidate for ADHD, selective serotonin re‑uptake inhibitors for comorbid anxiety, antipsychotics (e.g., risperidone) for severe aggression. Avoid benzodiazepines due to dependence risk.
Monitor for side effects: weight gain

sections.p: Regular follow‑up every 3–6 months to assess symptom trajectory, medication tolerance and family dynamics. Prevention focuses on early intervention in at‑risk children, strengthening family support, and community education on violence prevention.
